clinicalPearls: Deposition of calcium pyrophosphate crystals in cartilage and joints, causing several clinical patterns
Acute CPP crystal arthritis (pseudogout) presents as an acute monoarthritis, classically of the knee or wrist
Chondrocalcinosis is the radiographic finding of cartilage calcification, often of the knee menisci and wrist triangular fibrocartilage
Synovial fluid shows positively birefringent, rhomboid crystals, distinguishing it from gout
It may mimic osteoarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis or septic arthritis
Younger patients or florid disease should prompt a search for metabolic associations such as haemochromatosis, hyperparathyroidism and hypomagnesaemia
reference.pathophysiology: Calcium pyrophosphate deposition disease results from the formation and deposition of calcium pyrophosphate dihydrate crystals within articular cartilage and fibrocartilage, promoted by abnormal pyrophosphate metabolism and ageing cartilage. Shedding of crystals into the joint space triggers an acute inflammatory response (pseudogout), while chronic deposition contributes to a degenerative arthropathy. Metabolic disorders that alter pyrophosphate or mineral handling, such as haemochromatosis, hyperparathyroidism and hypomagnesaemia, predispose to earlier or more extensive disease.
additionalInvestigations: Synovial fluid analysis for crystals and to exclude infection
Screening for metabolic associations (ferritin/transferrin saturation, calcium and parathyroid hormone, magnesium)
Joint aspiration to exclude septic arthritis when acute
redFlags: Features indistinguishable from septic arthritis requiring aspiration
Young-onset or florid disease suggesting a metabolic cause
Systemic upset with an acutely hot joint
reference.prognosis: Acute attacks are self-limiting and treatable, but chronic CPPD can cause a progressive degenerative arthropathy; treating any underlying metabolic disorder is important.
pitfalls: Assuming an acute hot joint is CPPD without excluding infection
Confusing the crystals and management with gout
Missing haemochromatosis or hyperparathyroidism in young patients
Attributing joint damage solely to osteoarthritis
